The agrarian rebellion fractured from the political
revolution over a simple question of stolen property.
The Meeting: June 1911. Zapata meets the new President
Francisco I. Madero. Madero asks for patience and legal procedures.
The Confrontation: Zapata points his rifle directly at Madero's
gold watch chain.
If I took your watch by force, and later we met
armed with equal strength, would you have
the right to demand it back? That is exactly
what has happened in Morelos... The pueblos
demand immediate restitution.
The Result: Madero demands disarmament; Zapata returns to
the mountains.

Article 6 (Restitution)

The Method
The Motive
Neither died in open battle. Both were lured into elaborately staged traps engineered and
funded by the highest levels of the federal government.
The new state required a total monopoly on violence and political power. The mere
existence of Zapata and Villa as living symbols of the agrarian poor remained an
existential threat to the capitalist state.

They lost the battlefield, but the revolution's most radical
demands became the foundation of modern Mexico.

The 1917 Constitution
The demands of the defeated peasant armies force
the inclusion of Article 27, establishing the nation's
permanent right to expropriate land and distribute ejidos.
The Land Reform
The victorious central state is forced to legalize
the Zapatista land distributions in Morelos just to
maintain peace and legitimacy.
The Paradox
The state murdered the caudillos. but was utterly
forced to adopt their radical social program in order
to survive.

The men were buried, but the myth of the peasant
in arms became an unkillable political force.
Cardenismo
¡ZAPATA VIVE!
When Zapata's body was displayed,
the campesinos refused to believe
it was him, claiming he was still
riding in the mountains.
For a century, whenever the state
failed the rural poor, the specter of
Earth and Steel returned to demand
the debt be paid.
The revolution never truly ended; it
merely changed its battlegrounds.
